Phone storage full: calculate the gap before deleting photos

By KYD Editorial · First published 2026-07-12 · Last editorial review 2026-10-05

English edition adapted on 2026-10-05. The original source-check date is retained below; this is not a fresh product or match investigation.

First calculate the extra space you need, then start with files you can replace. The numbers below are planning examples—not measurements from a tested phone or a manufacturer’s free-space requirement.

A 128GB example with 8GB free

Read total and available storage from the device settings using the same units. Advertised capacity and currently usable storage are not interchangeable, and RAM is a separate category. If you choose a 15% free-space planning target, 128 × 0.15 = 19.2GB. With 8GB already free, the additional target is 19.2 − 8 = 11.2GB. The 15% figure is a user-selected planning assumption, not a universal manufacturer recommendation or an update-installation requirement.

Chosen free-space targetTarget free spaceExtra space from 8GB free
10%12.8GB4.8GB
15%19.2GB11.2GB
20%25.6GB17.6GB

Compare these inputs in the storage planner. It deletes nothing. If an update is your goal, inspect that update’s actual requirements instead of assuming a chosen percentage is sufficient.

Different cleanup buttons remove different things

ActionPossible effectCheck first
Delete downloaded mediaRemoves the device’s offline copyCan your account or subscription download it again?
Clear cacheRemoves temporary files that may returnIs this distinct from clearing app data?
Clear app data or storageCan remove local state, logins and dataApp-specific backup and recovery access
Clean messenger attachmentsCan remove files that cannot be downloaded againWhether the conversation backup includes media
Ordinary photo deletionMay affect cloud copies and other devicesThe service’s sync and trash behavior

Do not rely only on “backup enabled”

  1. Verify the account receiving the photos.
  2. Inspect recent and older photos plus important long videos; a sample does not prove every item is backed up.
  3. Where possible, open actual files through the service on another device rather than checking thumbnails alone.
  4. Inspect pending, paused or failed uploads.
  5. Read the scope of the service’s device-space function before using it.

Google Photos’ Free up space differs from ordinary deletion. Do not assume iCloud or another app behaves identically. Keep important originals in an independent copy outside the synchronized library and open that copy. See the photo-backup guide.

Reach the target in stages

In the illustrative 11.2GB gap, removing 4GB of replaceable offline video and 1.5GB of unnecessary downloads yields 5.5GB, leaving 5.7GB. Clearing 0.8GB of cache still leaves 4.9GB. Re-read available storage after each step: trash retention and new temporary files can mean the observed gain differs from the arithmetic. Do not jump to deleting all photos because a cache cleanup was small.

If the space still does not add up

Record total and free space, the three largest apps, each cleanup action and before/after values. Do not delete unknown system folders. Allow storage analysis to settle after a restart and consult manufacturer guidance. Factory reset is a separate decision requiring verified backup and account-recovery access.

A document-looking filename may hide another ending. Showing extensions helps you read the complete name without opening the file, but it is not a file-format or malware test.

Enable the display and check the result

In Windows 11 File Explorer, use View → Show → File name extensions. In the Windows 10 ribbon interface, use the View tab’s File name extensions checkbox. These instructions are based on Microsoft documentation; this article does not present original Windows screenshots.

  1. Open a folder with a document whose source you know.
  2. Enable extensions and confirm that the ending such as .pdf or .docx is visible.
  3. Widen the Name column if the ending is truncated, or select the file once to inspect its full name. Do not double-click just to check.
  4. Compare the ending, sender and file type you actually expected.

The setting changes display, not file contents. Special formats such as shortcuts may also require checking Properties and the target.

Six illustrative filenames

These English filenames adapt the original educational examples. They are strings, not downloadable files or actual malware samples.

Full nameClueNext check
notice.pdfShown with a PDF extensionThe contents and sender remain unverified
notice.pdf.exeThe final extension is .exeDo not run an unexpected executable as a document
minutes.final.docxThe last extension is .docxSeveral dots alone do not establish danger
budget.xlsmA macro-enabled Excel formatVerify any request to enable content
material.pdf.lnkA shortcut filenameInspect the actual target separately

Extension, icon, contents and signature are different

An extension helps the operating system select an app. The icon is also influenced by associations and settings. Both can change without converting the underlying data, so neither proves the real format. A signature can provide publisher information, but is not permission to run any file. Many documents have no signature tab; its absence alone does not prove malware.

Older .doc, .xls and .ppt formats can contain macros too. Do not ignore a warning solely because the filename does not end in .docm.

Practice without uploading files

Enter the examples in the filename and extension checker. Compare notice.pdf.exe with minutes.final.docx. The tool reads strings only; it does not test Explorer or detect malware. The tool verification notes publish its test scope.

If you renamed or ran the file

If you changed an extension on your own file and know its original name, restore it. Do not guess different extensions on an unknown file to make it open. Obtain the original from the sender or convert it using the producing app’s export function. Downloading is different from executing or installing. If unwanted apps appeared after execution, use the download-warning response guide or your organization’s support process, not a name-only check.

Use Snipping Tool for more control

Find Snipping Tool through Start. Select an available region, window or delay option that fits the situation. A delayed capture can help when a temporary menu must be visible. Use the tool’s save or copy controls and verify where the result went.

Keep enough error context

A useful report includes the error text and enough of the app or nearby controls to explain where it happened. Cropping too tightly can remove the clue; capturing the entire desktop can expose unrelated information. If a sequence matters, provide separate labeled screenshots for the starting location, error and action rather than one crowded image.

Check privacy around the edges

Inspect the browser address bar, account name, notifications, file paths, tabs, bookmarks, conversations and taskbar. Names and private folder labels can appear far from the error itself. Crop unnecessary material or fully cover sensitive details with an opaque block.

Reopen the actual sharing copy

Save and inspect the final exported image, not only the editing view. Ensure that you are sharing the redacted copy rather than the original. Use descriptive filenames with a date and non-sensitive issue label, and verify every image if you attach several. See the screenshot privacy checklist for codes, locations and hidden context.

Manage retained screenshots

Keep files only as long as needed and according to applicable organizational rules. On a shared computer, avoid leaving private captures on the desktop or in Downloads after the task. Useful documentation should show the problem without exposing unrelated people’s information.
